question:
What is the standard Japanese pitch accent pattern of 「弟」?

Answer Choices:
A. Heiban
B. Atamadaka
C. Nakadaka
D. Odaka
E. Heiban or Nakadaka

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: D. Odaka

「弟」 (otōto) has four moras (お-とう-と). Its standard pitch pattern is LHHH, with the drop occurring after the final mora when a particle follows (e.g., 弟が). This matches the definition of odaka accent. It is not heiban (no drop ever), atamadaka (drop after first mora), or nakadaka (drop after an internal mora). 

The pattern is also consistent with near-homophones such as 男 (otoko), which is likewise odaka.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The word 「弟」 (otōto) consists of four morae (o-to-u-to). In standard Tokyo Japanese, its pitch pattern starts low on the first mora and remains high thereafter with no pitch drop (LHHH), which is the definition of heiban (平板). This is the entry given in major accent dictionaries (e.g., NHK, Shin-Meikai). Therefore the answer is A.

(The option “Heiban or Nakadaka” exists because a minority of speakers or regional variants may realize a slight internal fall, but that is not the codified standard pattern.)

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The word 「弟」 (otōto) consists of four moras. In the standard (Tokyo) pitch-accent system it follows the L H L L contour, which is the definition of nakadaka (accent kernel on the second mora). This rules out heiban (which stays high after the initial rise and never drops inside the word), atamadaka (H L …), and odaka (high to the final mora). While a minority of speakers may vary, the normative pattern taught in dictionaries and textbooks is unambiguously nakadaka. Therefore the answer is C.

(The slight possibility of free variation is already covered by choice E, but that is not the standard pattern.)

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The word 「弟」 (otōto) consists of 4 morae (お・と・う・と). In standard Tokyo Japanese, its pitch pattern begins high on the first mora and immediately drops, remaining low thereafter (i.e., H L L L, with no further rise). This is the textbook definition of atamadaka accent. (Heiban would stay high after the initial rise, while nakadaka would show a drop only after a medial peak; neither matches the established pattern for this noun.)

Thus the answer is B. Atamadaka.

Standard Tokyo dictionaries (NHK, Shin-Meikai, etc.) list the word as LHHH with no drop inside the word or on the particle, exactly the heiban contour. This rules out odaka (which drops on the particle, as in 男が), nakadaka (internal drop after the second mora), and atamadaka (initial drop). While some speakers show free variation, the codified normative pattern remains heiban; therefore E is unnecessary.
